title: Bacterial vaginosis: understanding discharge and getting the right assessment
intro: Bacterial vaginosis, or BV, involves a change in the balance of bacteria in the vagina. It can cause an unusual discharge or smell, while some people have no symptoms. It is not evidence of being unclean or of a partner's infidelity. Similar symptoms can come from other conditions, so recognising a familiar smell is not enough to diagnose every episode or choose treatment safely.

sections.heading: Describe the symptoms without assuming the cause
paragraphs: A thin greyish or whitish discharge and a fishy smell may occur, sometimes more noticeable after sex. Marked itching, soreness, sores or pain can suggest another or additional problem. Thrush, irritation and sexually transmitted infections need different consideration. Tell the clinician when the change began, whether it has happened before and about any pain, bleeding, pregnancy or new sexual exposure. You do not need to apologise for discussing these symptoms.

sections.heading: Know what an appointment may involve
paragraphs: A clinician asks about symptoms and may offer an examination or a sample of discharge to help distinguish BV from other causes. Testing for sexually transmitted infections may be relevant depending on circumstances; BV and another infection can coexist. You can ask why an examination is needed, request an appropriate interpreter or support and discuss consent before proceeding. A previous diagnosis does not automatically establish the cause of a new episode.

sections.heading: Follow a treatment chosen for your situation
paragraphs: Treatment may involve prescribed antibiotics taken by mouth or used locally. The choice depends on the circumstances, including pregnancy, other medicines and previous treatment. Use the prescribed course and ask about side effects, missed doses and any precautions involving alcohol, sex or contraception. Do not substitute leftover antibiotics or repeatedly use a thrush treatment without confirming the cause. Contact the prescriber if symptoms persist, worsen or return instead of extending treatment yourself.

sections.heading: Make recurrence a reason for review, not blame
paragraphs: BV can recur even after appropriate treatment. Keep a record of episodes, prescribed courses and possible associations with periods, sexual activity or products. Ask whether further testing, a different strategy or partner assessment is appropriate under current advice for your situation. Recommendations can depend on the pattern of recurrence and the partnership. Avoid vaginal douching, deodorants or improvised internal remedies; these can disturb or irritate the area rather than reliably restore its bacterial balance.

sections.heading: Seek earlier help for pregnancy or warning signs
paragraphs: If you are pregnant or could be and develop unusual discharge, discuss it with a maternity professional or clinician rather than self-treating. Pelvic pain, fever, significant bleeding, severe pain or feeling very unwell needs prompt assessment and should not be assumed to be uncomplicated BV. Severe illness or collapse requires emergency help. If symptoms resolve, ask whether any follow-up is needed; do not assume every person needs the same testing or treatment schedule.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: avoiding the wrong repeated treatment
examples.text: Someone notices an unfamiliar discharge and smell but little itching. Instead of repeatedly buying antifungal treatment, they seek assessment and describe the symptoms, pregnancy possibility and any new exposure. They ask which causes and tests are relevant rather than diagnosing themselves from the smell alone.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: discussing recurrence constructively
examples.text: A person has symptoms again after completing a prescribed course. They bring dates and medicine details to the appointment and ask about confirmation, prevention and whether partner assessment matters. They do not assume recurrence proves poor hygiene or wrongdoing by either partner.

questions: Do the findings support BV, or should another cause or a coexisting infection be checked?
Which treatment and precautions are appropriate for my pregnancy status and medicines?
If symptoms return, what should we reassess and is partner assessment relevant?
